backref.label: Back-reference
backref.named.long: Matches the same text that the named group "{ref}" matched earlier.
backref.numeric.long: Matches the same text that capture group #{ref} matched earlier.
canvas.breakdown.hint: Hover to highlight, click to select, double-click to open reference.
canvas.choice.heading: Choice between:
canvas.description.label: DESCRIPTION
canvas.empty.title: Drag elements here
canvas.keyboardHint: Use left and right arrow keys to move between nodes. Home and End jump to the first or last node. Delete removes the selected node. Escape clears the selection. Plus, minus, and zero control zoom.
canvas.literalRun.expandAria: Run of {count} literal characters: {chars}. Click to expand.
character.escaped.label: Escaped character
character.label: Character
character.quoted.long: Matches "{value}" literally — everything inside \Q…\E is taken as plain text.
choice.label: Alternation
choice.long: Matches any one of {count, plural, one {# alternative} other {# alternatives}}.
class.posix.label: POSIX {name}
class.posix.long: POSIX bracket class — matches any character in the {name} class.
class.posix.negated.label: Non-POSIX {name}
class.posix.negated.long: POSIX bracket class — matches any character NOT in the {name} class.
class.range.label: Range
class.range.long: Matches any character from "{from}" to "{to}" (char codes {fromCode}–{toCode}).
conditional.cond.recursion.any: if currently inside any recursive call
conditional.label: Conditional
conditional.long: Runs the yes branch {condLabel}; otherwise runs the no branch. PCRE, Perl, .NET only.
construct.anchor.end.label: End anchor
construct.anchor.end.long: Marks the end of the input — or the end of any line with the /m flag.
construct.anchor.endOfString.label: End of string
construct.anchor.endOfString.long: Marks the end of the input. May allow a single trailing newline.
construct.anchor.endOfStringOnly.label: Absolute end of string
construct.anchor.endOfStringOnly.long: Marks the absolute end of the input — no trailing newline allowed.
construct.anchor.matchReset.label: Match-reset anchor
construct.anchor.matchReset.long: Throws away everything matched so far — the rest of the pattern becomes the actual match. A "lookbehind without lookbehind" trick. PCRE, Java, Perl. Not in JavaScript.
construct.anchor.matchStart.label: Match-start anchor
construct.anchor.matchStart.long: Marks where the previous match ended, or the start of the string for the first match. PCRE, Java, Python, Ruby, .NET, Rust. Not in JavaScript.
construct.anchor.nonWordBoundary.label: Non-word boundary
construct.anchor.nonWordBoundary.long: Marks a position that is NOT at the edge of a word.
construct.anchor.start.label: Start anchor
construct.anchor.start.long: Marks the start of the input — or the start of any line with the /m flag.
construct.anchor.startOfString.label: Start of string
construct.anchor.startOfString.long: Marks the very beginning of the input. Ignores the /m line-mode flag.
construct.anchor.wordBoundary.label: Word boundary
construct.anchor.wordBoundary.long: Marks the edge of a word — where a letter, digit, or underscore meets anything else.
construct.choice.separator.label: OR
construct.choice.separator.long: Matches the expression before or after the |.
construct.class.negated.label: Negated set
construct.class.negated.long: Matches any one character NOT listed inside the brackets.
construct.class.set.label: Character set
construct.class.set.long: Matches any one character from inside the brackets.
construct.class.setop.difference.label: Set difference
construct.class.setop.difference.long: Matches characters in the first set excluding those in the second set (set subtraction). Java, .NET, Rust, Python regex module.
construct.class.setop.difference.short: In the first set but not the second:
construct.class.setop.intersection.label: Set intersection
construct.class.setop.intersection.long: Matches only characters present in both sets (set intersection). Java, .NET, Rust, Python regex module.
construct.conditional.no.label: No branch
construct.conditional.no.long: Runs when the condition is false.
construct.conditional.yes.label: Yes branch
construct.conditional.yes.long: Runs when the condition is true.
construct.dot.label: Dot
construct.dot.long: Matches any single character except line breaks.
construct.element.fallback.label: Element
construct.esc.0.label: Null
construct.esc.0.long: Matches the NUL character (U+0000). Followed by more digits it becomes an octal escape in Perl, PCRE and Ruby.
construct.esc.B.label: Non-word boundary
construct.esc.B.long: Marks a position that is NOT at the edge of a word.
construct.esc.B.short: Position NOT at a word edge.
construct.esc.D.label: Non-Digit
construct.esc.D.long: Matches any character that isn't a digit.
construct.esc.D.short: Anything that is not a digit.
construct.esc.H.label: Non-horizontal whitespace
construct.esc.H.long: Matches any character that isn't horizontal whitespace. In Ruby (Onigmo) \H means "not a hexadecimal digit" instead.
construct.esc.R.label: Unicode line break
construct.esc.R.long: Matches any line break sequence — \r\n, \n, \r, NEL, LS, PS. PCRE, Java, Perl, Ruby.
construct.esc.S.label: Non-Whitespace
construct.esc.S.long: Matches any character that isn't whitespace.
construct.esc.V.label: Non-vertical whitespace
construct.esc.V.long: Matches any character that isn't vertical whitespace — anything but the vertical tab (U+000B) in Python and Ruby, and anything outside the whole vertical-whitespace class in PCRE, PHP, Perl and Java.
construct.esc.W.label: Non-Word
construct.esc.W.long: Matches any character that isn't a letter, digit, or underscore.
construct.esc.X.label: Extended grapheme cluster
construct.esc.X.long: Matches one user-perceived character — possibly several code points (e.g. base letter + combining marks, or an emoji sequence). PCRE, Java, Perl, Ruby, .NET.
construct.esc.b.label: Word boundary
construct.esc.b.long: Marks the edge of a word — between a word character (\w) and anything else (\W).
construct.esc.b.short: Position at the edge of a word.
construct.esc.d.label: Digit
construct.esc.f.label: Form feed
construct.esc.h.label: Horizontal whitespace
construct.esc.h.long: Matches horizontal whitespace — space, tab, and their Unicode relatives. In Ruby (Onigmo) \h means a hexadecimal digit instead. PCRE, PHP, Perl, Java, Elixir.
construct.esc.h.short: Space or tab — a hex digit in Ruby.
construct.esc.n.label: Newline
construct.esc.r.label: Carriage return
construct.esc.s.label: Whitespace
construct.esc.s.long: Matches any whitespace — spaces, tabs, newlines, and other invisible characters.
construct.esc.t.label: Tab
construct.esc.v.label: Vertical whitespace
construct.esc.v.long: Matches a vertical tab (U+000B) in JavaScript, Python and Ruby. In PCRE, PHP, Perl and Java it matches the whole vertical-whitespace class — line feed, vertical tab, form feed, carriage return, NEL, LS, PS.
construct.esc.v.short: Vertical tab — the whole class in PCRE.
construct.esc.w.label: Word
construct.esc.w.long: Matches any letter, digit, or underscore — equivalent to [a-zA-Z0-9_].
construct.group.absent.label: Absent operator
construct.group.absent.long: Matches the longest string that doesn't contain the enclosed pattern. Onigmo, Ruby only.
construct.group.absent.short: Longest string NOT containing the pattern.
construct.group.atomic.label: Atomic group
construct.group.atomic.long: Locks in whatever this group matches — the engine won't backtrack into it. Used to prevent catastrophic backtracking. PCRE, Java, Ruby, Perl, .NET, Rust.
construct.group.branchReset.label: Branch reset group
construct.group.branchReset.long: Each alternative inside reuses the same capture-group numbers, so `(?|(a)|(b))` has a single group #1 regardless of which branch matched. PCRE and Perl only.
construct.group.nonCapturing.label: Non-capturing group
construct.group.nonCapturing.long: Groups a section so quantifiers and alternation apply to the whole thing — without saving what it matched.
construct.lookaround.lookahead.label: Positive lookahead
construct.lookaround.lookahead.long: Checks that the text ahead matches this pattern, without consuming any characters.
construct.lookaround.lookahead.negated.l: Checks that the text ahead does NOT match this pattern, without consuming any characters.
construct.lookaround.lookbehind.label: Positive lookbehind
construct.lookaround.lookbehind.long: Checks that the text just before matches this pattern, without consuming any characters.
Checks that the text just before does NOT match this pattern, without consuming any characters.
construct.subroutine.recursion.label: Recursion
construct.subroutine.recursion.long: Re-runs the entire pattern from the current position — used to match nested or self-similar structures like balanced parentheses. PCRE, Perl, Ruby.
describe.anchor.matchReset: reset match start (drop earlier captured text)
describe.backref.pattern.named: the pattern of group named "{ref}" recursively
describe.choice.eitherWithMore: either {first} or {second} (and {n, plural, one {# other alternative} other {# other alternatives}})
describe.class.exceptMany: any character except certain special characters
describe.class.unicode.neg: a character NOT in Unicode property {name}
describe.escape.N: any character except a newline — but simply the letter N in JavaScript and Ruby
describe.escape.R: a Unicode line break — but simply the letter R in JavaScript
describe.escape.X: an extended grapheme cluster — but simply the letter X in JavaScript
describe.escape.h.neg: not horizontal whitespace — in Ruby, not a hex digit
describe.escape.h.pos: horizontal whitespace — but a hex digit in Ruby
describe.escape.v.neg: not a vertical tab — in PCRE, not vertical whitespace
describe.escape.v.pos: a vertical tab — but the whole vertical-whitespace class in PCRE
describe.quant.fuzzy: {bare} (approximate match, up to {max, plural, one {# {type, select, s {substitution} i {insertion} d {deletion} other {error}}} other {# {type, select, s {substitutions} i {insertions} d {deletions} other {errors}}}})
describe.quant.fuzzy.unbounded: {bare} (approximate match, any number of {type, select, s {substitutions} i {insertions} d {deletions} other {errors}})
describe.truncated: … [+{n, plural, one {# more char} other {# more chars}}; complex pattern]
esc.unknown.label: Escape
group.balancing.label: Balancing group (pop "{name}")
group.balancing.long: Pops the most recent capture of "{name}" off its stack. Paired with a push group `(?<{name}>…)`, this matches balanced constructs like nested parens. .NET only.
group.capturing.label: Capturing group
group.capturing.long: Wraps a section and saves whatever it matches as group #{index}, so you can reference or extract it later.
group.named.label: Named group
group.named.long: Wraps a section and saves whatever it matches under the name "{name}", so you can reference or extract it later.
group.scopedFlags.label: Scoped inline flags
group.scopedFlags.long: Applies the flags `{on}{off}` only to the enclosed section — flags outside this group are unaffected.
help.alternation.desc: The pipe character | means "OR". The regex tries the left side first; if it fails, it tries the right. cat|dog matches either. Combine with groups: (Mon|Tue|Wed)day matches "Monday", "Tuesday", or "Wednesday".
help.anchor.desc: ^ matches the position at the very beginning of the text (or each line with the /m flag). $ matches the end. They match positions, not characters. Combine to validate entire strings: ^\d'{'5'}'$ for exactly 5 digits.
help.anchor.label: Start / End anchor
help.atomic.desc: Groups like (?:…) but once matched, the engine won’t backtrack into the group. Prevents catastrophic backtracking. (?>a+)b fails instantly on "aaaa" instead of retrying every substring.
help.backref.desc: Refers back to what a capturing group already matched, requiring the SAME text to appear again. (\w+)\s+\1 matches repeated words like "the the". The number is the group position. Named groups use \k<name> in most flavors — Python spells it (?P=name), and PostgreSQL has no named-backreference syntax at all.
help.balancing.desc: .NET-exclusive feature for matching balanced constructs. (?<open>\() captures a "push", (?<-open>\)) captures a "pop" and fails if the stack is empty. Enables regex to match balanced parentheses, brackets, etc.
help.balancing.label: Balancing group
help.bell.desc: \a matches the BEL (alert/bell) control character (ASCII 0x07), historically used to trigger a terminal beep. Like \e, it is not universal: dart, javascript and typescript treat \a as an identity escape — it matches the literal letter “a” instead.
help.bell.label: Bell / Alert (BEL)
help.boundary.desc: Matches the invisible boundary between a word character and a non-word character. \bcat\b matches "cat" as a whole word but not "category". \B is the opposite — where there is NO word boundary.
help.branchReset.desc: Resets the group-numbering counter at each alternative so both sides use the same numbers. (?|(cat)|(dog)) puts either capture in group 1. Useful when you want unified access to alternatives regardless of which branched matched.
help.class.desc: Matches ONE character from the list inside the brackets. [aeiou] matches any vowel. Ranges: [a-z] is any lowercase letter. Add ^ at start to negate: [^0-9] is anything except digits.
help.class.label: Character class
help.classDifference.desc: Inside a character class, -- matches everything in the left set EXCEPT what is in the right one. [a-z--[aeiou]] matches lowercase consonants. Narrower support than &&: Rust and ICU (Swift, MySQL) honor it, while Java and Ruby read -- as a literal dash and match everything with no error — use [a-z&&[^aeiou]] there instead.
help.classDifference.label: Class difference
help.classIntersection.desc: Inside a character class, && restricts matching to characters that are in BOTH sides. [a-z&&[^aeiou]] matches lowercase consonants (all lowercase letters AND not vowels). [\p'{'L'}'&&\p'{'ASCII'}'] matches letters that are also ASCII.
help.classIntersection.label: Class intersection
help.conditional.desc: Picks one of two patterns based on whether a capture group matched. (?(1)yes|no) uses "yes" if group 1 captured, otherwise "no". Advanced but powerful for context-sensitive parsing.
help.controlEscape.desc: \cX matches a control character, computed from the letter X: its code point is X''s own ASCII value with the top three bits cleared (X & 0x1F). \cA matches Ctrl-A (ASCII 0x01, "start of heading"); \cJ matches a line feed the same way \n does.
help.controlEscape.label: Control character escape
help.digit.desc: \d matches any number from 0 to 9. \D matches anything that is NOT a digit. For example, \d'{'3'}' matches exactly three digits like "123" or "007".
help.digit.label: Digit / Non-digit
help.dot.desc: Matches any single character — a letter, digit, symbol, or space. The only thing it won’t match is a newline (unless you enable the /s flag). Useful as a wildcard: "a.c" matches "abc", "a1c", "a-c", etc.
help.endString.desc: \z matches only the very end of input, regardless of flags. \Z matches end of input OR just before a trailing newline — useful when input files end with \n.
help.escape.desc: A backslash before a special character makes it literal. \. matches a real dot, \+ a literal plus. Also used for invisible characters: \n (newline), \t (tab), \r (carriage return), \0 (null).
help.escape.label: Escape sequences
help.escapeChar.desc: \e matches the ESC control character (ASCII 0x1B), used to start ANSI terminal escape sequences. Supported in most flavors as a genuine single-character escape; in dart, javascript and typescript \e is not special at all — it is an “identity escape” that just matches the literal letter “e”.
help.escapeChar.label: Escape character (ESC)
help.flag.E.desc: ERE mode — extended regex syntax (grep -E / sed -E). The default for this flavor.
help.flag.U.desc: Ungreedy — swap greedy / lazy quantifier defaults.
help.flag.d.desc: Indices — records start/end offsets for every capture group.
help.flag.g.desc: Global — find all matches, not just the first.
help.flag.m.desc: Multiline — ^ and $ match line boundaries. In Ruby, m means dotAll instead.
help.flag.n.desc: Newline handling — in MySQL, n makes dot match newlines (dotAll). In PostgreSQL, n instead makes dot exclude newlines and lets ^ and $ match at line boundaries.
help.flag.y.desc: Sticky — each match must start exactly where the last one ended.
help.flags.intro: Toggle flags using the buttons in the toolbar. Active flags are shown in blue.
help.formFeed.desc: \f matches a form feed character (ASCII 0x0C). Rare in modern text, but still occasionally used as a page-break marker in printed or legacy documents. Universally supported.
help.formFeed.label: Form feed
help.grapheme.desc: Matches an extended Unicode grapheme cluster — a full "user-perceived character" which may be composed of multiple code points (e.g. a base letter plus combining accent, or an emoji with modifiers). Treat as "one visible character" for humans.
help.group.desc: Wraps part of your pattern in parentheses to treat it as a unit AND remember what it matched. The captured text can be reused later with \1, \2, etc. Example: (\d'{'4'}')-(\d'{'2'}') captures the year and month separately from "2024-03".
help.group.label: Capturing group
help.hexBraceEscape.desc: \x'{'H...'}' matches the character with the given hex code point, with as many digits as needed — unlike \xHH, not limited to two. \x'{'263A'}' matches ☺ (SMILING FACE). Reaches far beyond ASCII where the plain \xHH form is capped at 0xFF.
help.hexBraceEscape.label: Hex escape (braced)
help.hexEscape.desc: \xHH matches the character with hex code point HH, always exactly two digits (0x00-0xFF). \x41 matches "A". Supported by every flavor, making it the most portable way to write a specific character by code point.
help.hexEscape.label: Hex escape (2-digit)
help.horizontal.desc: Matches horizontal whitespace — spaces, tabs, and other horizontal separators. More restrictive than \s (which includes line breaks). \H matches everything except horizontal whitespace.
help.horizontal.label: Horizontal whitespace
help.lineBreak.desc:
Matches any Unicode line-break sequence as a single unit — 
, 
, , \v,  , U+0085, U+2028, U+2029. Equivalent to (?:
|[
\v \x'{'85'}'\x'{'2028'}'\x'{'2029'}']). Use when splitting or normalizing text across operating systems.
help.literal.desc: Matches the exact characters you type. For example, "cat" only matches the word "cat". Special characters like . or + are automatically escaped when you drag them onto the canvas.
help.literal.label: Literal text
help.lookaround.desc: Checks if something exists before or after the current position WITHOUT matching it. (?=\d) lookahead: "the next character must be a digit". (?<=@) lookbehind: "the previous character must be @". Add ! to negate: (?!\d) "must NOT be followed by a digit".
help.lookaround.label: Lookahead / Lookbehind
help.matchReset.desc: Resets the match start position. Everything before \K is matched but discarded from the final result. Equivalent to a variable-length lookbehind. Example: foo\Kbar matches "foobar" but only "bar" is the returned match.
help.matchStart.desc: Anchors the match to the position where the previous match ended. Useful with /g flag to ensure matches are contiguous. Fails if the engine has skipped characters since the last match.
help.named.desc: Like a regular capturing group but accessible by name rather than number. (?<year>\d'{'4'}') captures 4 digits as "year". Reference with \k<year> (or (?P=year) in Python). Makes complex patterns self-documenting.
help.named.label: Named capturing group
help.namedCodePoint.desc: \N'{'U+HHHH'}' matches the character at the given Unicode code point, spelled out with the "U+" prefix used in Unicode charts and documentation. \N'{'U+0041'}' matches "A". Narrow support — only php, perl and elixir accept this spelling; everywhere else, use \x'{'...'}' or \u'{'...'}' for the same code point.
help.namedCodePoint.label: Named code point
help.newline.desc: \n matches a line feed (ASCII 0x0A, Unix line ending). \r matches a carriage return (ASCII 0x0D). Together \r\n matches a Windows line ending.
help.newline.label: Newline / Carriage return
help.noncapture.desc: Groups parts of your pattern together (so you can apply quantifiers or alternation to the whole group) but does NOT remember the match. Use for structural grouping without extracting the value: (?:http|https):// for the protocol options.
help.octalEscape.desc: A backslash followed by octal digits matches the character at that code point in base 8. Three admission rules, depending on flavor: bare \NNN, \0NN with a leading zero to disambiguate from a backreference, or braced \o'{'NNN'}'. A bare \NNN is octal only when no capture group has that number AND it has enough digits for the flavor: one in Dart, and in JavaScript and TypeScript without the u or v flag (\1; with u or v it is a syntax error), two in most other flavors (\12), three in Python (\101, which Python reads as octal even when group 101 exists). Anything shorter is a backreference, which the engine rejects when that group does not exist. \101 (or \0101, or \o'{'101'}') matches "A" (0o101 = 0x41 = 65).
help.octalEscape.label: Octal escape
help.posix.desc: Named character classes from the POSIX standard''s full 12-name set: [:alpha:], [:alnum:], [:digit:], [:space:], [:upper:], [:lower:], [:punct:], [:xdigit:] (hex), [:cntrl:], [:graph:], [:print:], [:blank:]. Only usable inside [...] brackets.
help.posix.label: POSIX character class
help.posixExtended.desc: Some engines also accept two non-standard POSIX names beyond the 12 above: [:ascii:] (any ASCII character) and [:word:] (letters, digits and underscore — the bracket-class equivalent of \w). Narrower support than the standard set: php, perl, ruby, rust and elixir honor them; other flavors that otherwise support POSIX names do not.
help.posixExtended.label: POSIX character class (extended names)
help.quantifier.desc: Control how many times the preceding element repeats. ? means 0 or 1 (optional). * means 0 or more. + means 1 or more. '{'3'}' exactly 3. '{'2,5'}' between 2 and 5. '{'3,'}' 3 or more. Add ? after for "lazy" (minimum match). Add + for "possessive" (no backtrack).
help.range.desc: Inside a character class, a hyphen defines a range between two characters by Unicode code point. [a-z] matches any lowercase letter, [0-9] any digit. Combine: [a-zA-Z0-9_] matches any "word" character.
help.range.label: Character range
help.relativeBackref.desc: PHP, Perl, R and Elixir also accept \g1, \g'{'1'}' and \g'{'-1'}' as a TEXT backreference — an alternate spelling for \1, not a subroutine call. \g'{'-1'}' counts backward from the most recently opened group, so it stays correct if you insert a group earlier in the pattern. Ruby is NOT included here: Onigmo reads \g1 as the literal characters "g1" rather than as a backreference at all.
help.relativeBackref.label: Relative backreference (\g)
help.replCase.desc: Wraps part of the replacement text to force it to uppercase between the start and end markers shown. Only a handful of flavors support an in-replacement case transform — for the rest, use the Replacement Builder''s transform pills instead, which apply the same effect outside the replacement string.
help.replCase.label: Case transform
help.replNamed.desc: Inserts the text captured by a named group, e.g. (?<year>\d'{'4'}'), by name instead of by position. Not every flavor can reference a named group in its replacement string — this row is hidden for flavors that can''t.
help.replNamed.label: Named group
help.replNumbered.desc: Inserts the text captured by a numbered group from the pattern. Group 1 is the first (...) in your regex, group 2 the second, and so on. The exact token shown depends on the flavor you''re testing against.
help.replNumbered.label: Numbered group
help.replPrePost.desc: Inserts the text immediately before ("pre-match") or immediately after ("post-match") the matched portion of the input. Useful for keeping surrounding context when replacing only part of a line. Only some flavors expose these tokens.
help.replPrePost.label: Before / after match
help.replWholeMatch.desc: Inserts the entire text the pattern matched, not just one captured group. Handy for wrapping or annotating a match without capturing it explicitly. A few flavors have no such token and must capture the whole pattern in a group instead — this row is hidden for those.
help.replWholeMatch.label: Whole match
help.rubyHexDigit.desc: In Ruby, \h matches ONE hexadecimal digit — the same as [0-9a-fA-F]. It is not horizontal whitespace: PCRE, Perl, Java and ICU all read \h as a space or tab, so an identical pattern quietly means something different depending on which engine runs it. \H matches any character that is not a hex digit. Ruby''s engine is Onigmo, which is where the difference comes from.
help.rubyHexDigit.label: Hex digit (Ruby)
help.scopedFlags.desc: Applies flags only to the enclosed subpattern. (?i:cat) matches "cat", "Cat", "CAT" case-insensitively while the rest of the pattern stays case-sensitive. (?-i:…) disables a flag locally.
help.scopedFlags.label: Scoped flag group
help.startString.desc: Matches ONLY the start of the entire input, never a line start — even with the /m flag. Use when you must anchor to the very beginning regardless of flags.
help.subroutine.desc: Re-invokes an earlier group as a subpattern, like calling a function. (?<n>[a-z]+)-(?&n) matches "abc-def". (?R) recurses into the entire pattern. Enables recursive grammars for balanced structures. Ruby''s Onigmo engine rejects this (?…) syntax entirely and spells the same call \g<name> instead — see "Subroutine call (\g<name>)" below.
help.subroutineRef.desc: Ruby''s Onigmo engine (plus PHP, R and Elixir) spells a subroutine call \g<name> or \g<1> instead of (?&name) — re-running the referenced group''s PATTERN, not its captured text. (a|b)\g<1> can match "ab" because the second \g<1> re-runs the alternation; a backreference to group 1 could only repeat whichever branch it first matched. Real Perl hard-errors on this exact spelling even though it supports subroutine calls via (?&name)/(?R).
help.subroutineRef.label: Subroutine call (\g<name>)
help.tab.desc: Matches a horizontal tab character (ASCII 0x09). Useful when parsing TSV files or indented content.
help.tab.label: Tab
help.tip.beSpecific.body: Instead of .*, use more specific classes like [a-z]* or \d*. This makes your regex faster and less prone to "catastrophic backtracking".
help.tip.beSpecific.title: Be specific
help.tip.lazy.body: By default, quantifiers like + and * are "greedy" and match as much as possible. Add a ? (e.g., +?) to make them "lazy" and match as little as possible.
help.tip.lazy.title: Lazy quantifiers
help.tip.startSimple.body: Break complex patterns into smaller, testable groups. Use the "Add Group" tool to isolate parts of your regex.
help.tip.startSimple.title: Start simple
help.tip.useAnchors.body: Always use ^ and $ if you want to validate the entire input string. Without them, a pattern like \d'{'3'}' will match "abc123def".
help.tip.useAnchors.title: Use anchors
help.unicode.desc: Matches characters by Unicode category or script. \p'{'L'}' matches any letter in any language. \p'{'Han'}' matches Chinese/Japanese characters. \p'{'N'}' any number, \p'{'P'}' punctuation. \P'{'…'}' is the inverse. Great for internationalized text.
help.unicode8Escape.desc: \UHHHHHHHH matches the character with the given hex code point, always exactly eight digits — covers the entire Unicode range (up to 0x10FFFF) in a single fixed-width escape. \U0001F600 matches 😀 (GRINNING FACE).
help.unicode8Escape.label: Unicode escape (8-digit)
help.unicodeBraceEscape.desc: \u'{'H...'}' matches the character with the given hex code point, braced and with as many digits as needed — reaching the full Unicode range in one escape instead of a \uHHHH surrogate pair. \u'{'1F600'}' matches 😀 (GRINNING FACE).
help.unicodeBraceEscape.label: Unicode escape (braced)
help.unicodeEscape.desc: \uHHHH matches the character with hex code point HHHH, always exactly four digits (the Unicode Basic Multilingual Plane, up to 0xFFFF). \u0041 matches "A". An astral code point above the BMP can be spelled as a UTF-16 SURROGATE PAIR — two \uHHHH escapes in a row — in flavors that support that spelling.
help.unicodeEscape.label: Unicode escape (4-digit)
help.unscopedFlags.desc: (?i) with no colon and no body turns on a flag for the rest of the pattern (or the rest of the current group) instead of wrapping a subpattern. Most flavors that support it accept it anywhere in the pattern, but python is stricter: CPython only allows a bare (?i) at position 0 — anywhere else it raises "global flags not at the start of the expression". Move it to the front, or switch to the scoped (?i:…) form if the flag needs to apply partway through.
help.unscopedFlags.label: Unscoped inline modifiers
help.vertical.desc: Matches vertical whitespace — line feeds, carriage returns, form feeds, vertical tabs. \V matches everything except vertical whitespace.
help.vertical.label: Vertical whitespace
help.verticalTab.desc: In this flavor, \v matches ONLY the vertical tab character (U+000B) — not line feeds, carriage returns, or form feeds. That''s narrower than the PCRE-family reading (PHP, Perl, Java and friends, plus R), where \v is widened to a whole vertical-whitespace class. Same two characters, two different meanings depending on which engine runs the pattern.
help.verticalTab.label: Vertical tab
help.whitespace.desc: \s matches invisible characters: spaces, tabs, and line breaks. \S matches anything visible. \s+ matches one or more spaces between words.
help.whitespace.label: Whitespace / Non-space
help.word.desc: \w matches any letter (a–z, A–Z), digit (0–9), or underscore (_). Think of it as "characters you’d use in a variable name". \W is the opposite.
help.word.label: Word / Non-word

ui.validation.atomicInLookbehind: Atomic group or possessive quantifier inside a lookbehind — move it outside the lookbehind, or make it an ordinary group or quantifier. JavaScript reads a lookbehind backwards, so this cannot be emulated there and would quietly match the wrong text
ui.validation.backrefMultiTokenEscape: This escape means one character followed by literal digits (\18 is character 1 then "8"), which cannot be combined with an atomic group or possessive quantifier here. Write the character escape explicitly, for example \x01 followed by 8
ui.validation.backrefNoGroupUnderUnicode: \1 refers to a capture group that does not exist, which the u and v flags make an error — add the group, or drop the flag. Without u it would not be a backreference at all but an escape for character 1
ui.validation.containerUpgradeRequired: Running regexes in a connected environment is available on the Pro tier.
ui.validation.emptyPattern: Empty pattern matches the empty string at every position
ui.validation.engine.constructUnsupporte: {engine} doesn't support the {construct} construct — rewrite the pattern to avoid it.
ui.validation.engine.duplicateGroupName: Two named groups in this pattern share the same name — group names must be unique.
ui.validation.engine.invalidSyntax: {engine} rejected this pattern as invalid regex syntax — see its exact message below.
ui.validation.engine.lookaroundUnsupport: {engine} doesn't support lookahead or lookbehind at all — rewrite the pattern to avoid them.
ui.validation.engine.lookbehindMustBeFix: {engine} requires lookbehind to be a fixed length — a range like a'{'1,5'}' is not allowed, though a long fixed one is.
ui.validation.engine.lookbehindNeedsMaxL: {engine} needs the lookbehind to have a maximum length it can work out — an open-ended one like a* will not compile.
ui.validation.engine.lookbehindTooLong: {engine} allows a lookbehind of at most {max} characters, and this one could be longer.
ui.validation.engineGaveUp: This pattern is too complex to evaluate — the engine stopped at its safety limit. No results to show.
ui.validation.js.duplicateGroupName: Duplicate group name — each named group must be unique
ui.validation.js.loneQuantifier: Unexpected quantifier — '{' '}' must follow something to repeat
ui.validation.js.nothingToRepeat: Quantifier has nothing to repeat — check *, +, ? placement
ui.validation.leadingQuantifier: A leading * has nothing to repeat — it must follow something to repeat
ui.validation.reversedQuantifier: Quantifier range is backwards — e.g. '{3,1}' should be '{1,3}'
ui.validation.reversedRange: Character class range is backwards — e.g. [z-a] should be [a-z]
ui.validation.shellEscape.backspace: {tool} matches {escape} as a backspace, not a word boundary — use {spelling} instead
ui.validation.shellEscape.backspaceNoFix: {tool} matches {escape} as a backspace, not a word boundary, and has no word-boundary spelling
ui.validation.shellEscape.literal: {tool} matches {escapes} as {count, plural, one {the literal character} other {literal characters}} — use {fixes} instead
ui.validation.shellEscape.literalNoFix: {tool} matches {escapes} as {count, plural, one {the literal character} other {literal characters}} — the backslash does nothing
ui.validation.subroutineChain: Subroutine references a group that itself calls another subroutine — not supported yet
ui.validation.subroutineInternalNumericR: Subroutine references a group whose body uses a numbered backreference to its own capture — engines disagree on what that means, so it is not supported
ui.validation.trailingBackslash: Pattern ends with a backslash — escape it as \\ or remove it
ui.validation.unnamedCaptureUnderN: Unnamed ( ) group under the n flag — name it, or turn n off. Under n it would not capture, and the canvas would still draw it as a capture group
ui.vscodeConflict.body: RegexPilot reloaded this pattern from the file's current version. Your canvas had changes the editor never confirmed.
ui.vscodeConflict.title: The file changed while you were disconnected
ui.vscodeSync.offlineTitle: Nothing is listening for edits to {file} — VS Code may be closed. Your changes are kept here and will be sent when it reconnects.
ui.vscodeSync.refusedTitle: This pattern uses Regex+ syntax (an atomic group or possessive quantifier) that the VS Code extension can't run, so this edit was not sent to {file}. Simplify the pattern to sync it.
ui.vscodeSync.rejectEditorRefused: The editor declined the change — the file may be read-only, or another extension blocked it.
ui.vscodeSync.rejectSpanInvalid: The editor could no longer find the regex this session was tracking. Edit again to retry.
ui.vscodeSync.rejectStaleBase: The file changed after your edit was sent, so the editor refused it. Edit again to retry against the current version.
ui.vscodeSync.rejectUnformattable: This pattern can't be written as a literal in this language without changing its meaning. Retrying won't help — simplify the pattern or edit the file directly.
ui.vscodeSync.syncingTitle: Proposing an edit to {file} — not yet confirmed by the editor
ui.workspaceCleared.body: Test sample, replace template and AI chat were reset. ⌘Z restores them.
ui.workspaceCleared.title: Workspace cleared
unicodeProperty.classChild.long: Matches any character with the Unicode property "{name}".
unicodeProperty.classChild.negated.long: Matches any character that does NOT have the Unicode property "{name}".
unicodeProperty.label: Unicode property
unicodeProperty.long: Matches any character with the Unicode property "{name}" — e.g. a category like Letter, a script like Han, or a block name. JavaScript (with /u), Python, PCRE, Perl, Ruby, Java, .NET, Rust.
unicodeProperty.negated.label: Negated Unicode property
unicodeProperty.negated.long: Matches any character that does NOT have the Unicode property "{name}". JavaScript (with /u), Python, PCRE, Perl, Ruby, Java, .NET, Rust.
